natural_language: A coastal power system represented by the IEEE case74ds faces an operational challenge: unusually warm seawater has reduced the effectiveness of nuclear plant cooling. As a result, these units must cut back their output, yet still sustain a relatively high minimum stable generation level to preserve reactor safety and thermal margins. These nuclear plants continue to run in a base-load posture with very limited flexibility, exhibiting extremely slow regulation capability. To ensure they remain prioritized in dispatch despite their constrained maneuverability, their grid access costs are lowered to reflect policy and reliability considerations. Set opf.violation to 1e-8, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

An urban distribution system represented by the IEEE 69-bus network is operating under an intense heat wave. Customer demand surges across residential zones, and reactive support needs rise in industrial areas as equipment runs harder and longer. At the same time, an older transmission corridor shows heightened electrical losses consistent with aging conductors, eroding transfer efficiency. To preserve thermal integrity, a critical tie line is temporarily derated, tightening available transfer capacity. With the system under stress, operators also relax the allowable lower voltage threshold at a vulnerable node to mitigate widespread alarms and maintain service continuity. Together, these conditions amplify congestion and voltage security risk, making an AC optimal power flow essential to balance supply, voltage, and line limits. Set opf.violation to 1e-7, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

The IEEE 118-bus system models a regional grid during an intense hydrological period. A major hydropower plant is required to rapidly empty storage ahead of an incoming flood peak. To accomplish this, it operates in a water-determined, forced generation mode with priority access to the grid, ensuring its output does not dip below a firm baseline. At the same time, river inflows across the region are abundant, pushing hydropower units toward high production. To avoid wasting water through spillage, these units aggressively lower their price offers so that the market dispatch fully absorbs their energy, prioritizing clean generation and reservoir management objectives over short-term cost signals. Configure the solver with tight feasibility tolerance and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code, similar to the few-shot example, using an AC OPF with a small violation threshold (set opf.violation to 1e-7) and the MIPS solver.

A compact regional grid is represented by the IEEE 9-bus test system variant (case9Q). During routine operations, a series compensation device on a key transmission corridor fails and is taken out of service. As a result, the affected path becomes electrically longer, which diminishes its ability to carry power and reduces overall transfer confidence on that route. In response, operators implement a conservative adjustment on a neighboring tie to preserve system security, reflecting tighter capacity limits while the network adapts to the equipment outage and maintenance investigation. Use MIPS as the ACOPF solver and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code, similar to the few-shot example.

A regional grid modeled with the IEEE 57-bus system faces a severe icing event brought on by persistent rain, snow, and freezing temperatures. Ice accretion on overhead lines drives up mechanical loading and raises the risk of conductor damage, prompting operators to reduce allowable transfer capability on stressed corridors to prevent breakage. Simultaneously, the harsh conditions degrade conductor performance, increasing electrical losses along impacted routes. Set a tight feasibility tolerance and use the MIPS AC OPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A compact regional network is represented by the IEEE 9-bus system. To push more power through a long transmission corridor while maintaining stability, the operator commissions series compensation along a key path, effectively shortening the electrical distance and improving the transfer limit. As a part of this upgrade, the corridor segments see improved capability and one link is cleared for higher throughput. This coordinated enhancement aims to unlock latent capacity while keeping flows secure and manageable across the grid. Set opf.violation to 1e-6, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

The IEEE 70-bus regional system (case70da) represents a grid operating during a flood management period. A hydropower station is instructed to run in a water-determined forced output mode to swiftly lower reservoir levels ahead of a forecasted peak, with guaranteed priority access to the network irrespective of energy costs. Concurrently, the system enters an abundant water season, where hydropower is plentiful. To avoid wasting water through spillage, the hydropower units reduce their market bids to extremely low levels to ensure full absorption of their output by the grid. Set the AC OPF solver to MIPS and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code as in the few-shot example.

A regional grid is represented with the IEEE 85-bus system. A severe sandstorm sweeps through the solar-rich areas, leaving a film of dust on photovoltaic arrays and dimming the available sunlight. As module surfaces become occluded, solar plants experience a marked decline in conversion efficiency and a notable reduction in their ability to support voltage. Operators respond by limiting the anticipated active output from the affected solar units and revising expectations for reactive support to preserve reliability under the harsh conditions. Set opf.violation to 1e-6, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A metropolitan grid is represented using the IEEE 18-bus system (case18). An extended spell of extreme heat drives record-breaking air conditioning use across the city, pushing active demand higher in dense commercial areas and reactive demand up along stressed distribution feeders. At the same time, high ambient temperatures force transformer equipment to operate with reduced transfer capability, narrowing margins on key corridors. The overheated conductors also exhibit increased electrical losses, further constraining the transmission paths. Meanwhile, rooftop photovoltaic installations limit their reactive support to protect power electronics from thermal stress, reducing available voltage support in parts of the network. To keep the system stable under these conditions, operators temporarily allow a more permissive minimum voltage threshold at a vulnerable node to avoid unnecessary curtailment. Use MIPS as the ACOPF solver and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code, similar to the few-shot example.

A compact regional grid is represented by the IEEE 5-bus system (case5). Global energy markets experience a sharp upswing in coal and natural gas prices, pushing thermal generation costs higher across the fleet. Operators anticipate increased marginal production expenses and steeper cost curves for key units, necessitating an economic re-optimization to reflect the new fuel landscape. In response, the market-clearing process is adjusted so the dispatch better internalizes elevated fuel costs for the affected generators. Use the MIPS AC OPF solver and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code, following the example format.

A compact utility subnetwork is represented using the IEEE 9-bus target system. During maintenance, the on-load tap changer of a key transformer suffers a mechanical lockout, preventing any automatic adjustments and leaving the tap held toward a lower position. This reduces the ability to support downstream voltages and narrows the operator’s margin for voltage regulation. To ride through the event, the operating team temporarily relaxes the minimum voltage tolerance at the upstream bus to maintain feasible dispatch while the equipment is secured and inspected. Use the AC optimal power flow with the MIPS solver and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code to reflect these conditions.

A regional distribution network is represented by the IEEE 22-bus system (case22). During a holiday midday lull, customer demand is unusually light while rooftop and community photovoltaic installations are producing at their peak. With local consumption depressed, surplus solar generation flows back into the grid, creating a pronounced reverse power flow that elevates voltage levels across parts of the system. Reactive demand dips at certain locations, further reducing local absorption and allowing voltage to rise. To contain overvoltage risks under these conditions, the operational strategy tightens the upper voltage limit at a sensitive node, ensuring that the system remains within safe bounds despite high distributed generation and low load. Set opf.violation to 1e-8, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A regional grid is represented by the IEEE 39-bus New England system (case39). Persistent haze reduces solar irradiance, causing a steep drop in photovoltaic output during daylight hours. At the same time, a stringent carbon pricing policy increases the operational costs for fossil-fueled plants and makes them less willing to run near their maximum capability. The combination of muted renewable generation and restrained thermal availability leaves the operator with a thin margin, where reserve levels are inadequate and regulation capability is stretched. To navigate this stressed condition, some thermal units are constrained to lower maximum production, reactive support capability is tightened at one unit to reflect equipment limits, and cost curves are adjusted upward to reflect the policy-induced increase in marginal generation costs. Set opf.violation to 1e-8, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

The regional grid is represented by the PEGASE 89-bus system during a holiday midday lull. Customer demand drops across the network, while widespread rooftop photovoltaic installations feed surplus power directly back into the transmission system. The combination of low consumption and strong distributed generation creates pronounced reverse power flows and pushes local voltages upward. To capture this situation, demand at select locations is reduced and the maximum allowable voltage in a critical area is tightened to mitigate the overvoltage risk and maintain secure operation during the low-load, high-PV period. Use MIPS as the ACOPF solver and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A distribution network is modeled using the IEEE 33-bus Baran–Wu system. Global energy markets undergo a sharp upswing in fuel costs, with coal and natural gas prices rising markedly. Thermal generators respond with higher production costs, which shifts their economic signals and affects commitment and dispatch decisions across the grid. To reflect this environment, specific generating units have their cost parameters adjusted upward to capture the increased fuel burden and the steeper economics of supplying energy. These changes are embedded into an AC optimal power flow to evaluate system operations under elevated fuel price conditions. Set opf.violation to 1e-08, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A large regional grid is represented by the case94pi system. A severe sandstorm sweeps across the area, coating photovoltaic arrays with dust and cutting the available sunlight. As the modules become occluded, the solar plants’ ability to produce active power diminishes sharply, and their capability to support voltage through reactive output is curtailed. Grid operators prepare for the reduced solar contribution by lowering expectations for the affected plants’ output and tightening their reactive support to maintain overall stability while the storm persists. Set opf.violation to 1e-8, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A regional grid is represented using the IEEE 141-bus system (case141). Long-term operation has led to conductor corrosion and wear on several transmission corridors, increasing electrical losses and diminishing performance. Concurrently, an extreme heat event elevates ambient temperatures, causing additional conductor sag. To maintain safe clearances under these conditions, system operators enforce more conservative thermal limits on impacted lines, effectively derating their allowable current. The combined effect of infrastructure aging and severe weather is a grid that must accommodate higher losses while operating under tighter line capacity constraints. Set opf.violation to 1e-6, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

The regional grid is represented by the IEEE 51-bus equivalent (case51he). A prolonged and extreme heat wave has pushed daytime air conditioning usage to new highs, especially in urban districts, straining the distribution network. At the same time, high ambient temperatures are forcing transformers to operate with reduced allowable loading, tightening transfer capability on critical corridors. A major photovoltaic plant is also affected: its inverters, limited by thermal stress, provide less reactive support, further reducing the system’s flexibility during peak demand. Operators allow deeper voltage dips at a stressed load area to keep the system secure during these conditions, while transmission conductors run hotter and exhibit increased losses along a key route. Set opf.violation to 1e-7, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A regional grid is represented by the IEEE 30-bus variant with reactive power data (case30Q). A virtual power plant aggregates distributed storage and flexible demand, responding to dispatch instructions to shave peaks and fill valleys while offering auxiliary voltage support. Through coordinated demand-side actions, participating customers actively reduce both active and reactive consumption during stressed periods, which alleviates congestion and improves local voltage safety margins. Operators also tighten the minimum acceptable voltage at a critical node to reinforce security under the VPP’s supportive posture. Set opf.violation to 1e-8, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

An offshore wind farm cluster is modeled using the case118zh network, representing both the collection grid at sea and the export links to shore. A persistent period of dense salt fog increases surface contamination on insulators and associated equipment, altering their effective electrical behavior. One of the longer export segments begins to exhibit noticeably higher losses, while a separate corridor must be operated with a tighter loading margin to preserve reliability under these harsh conditions. In addition, a submarine cable span shows stronger charging effects due to moisture and contamination. System operators prepare the network for these environmental stresses by adjusting line characteristics and transfer capabilities while coordinating wind farm injections and onshore support to maintain secure and economical operation. Set opf.violation to 1e-7, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A regional transmission system is modeled using the IEEE RTS 24-bus network (case24_ieee_rts). Large data center clusters are placed into full-load operation, pushing up baseline electricity usage and tightening expectations for service quality. At the same time, growth in high-precision digital industries introduces equipment that is exceptionally sensitive to voltage excursions, requiring the grid to maintain a tighter delivery band to avoid both transient spikes and steady deviations. Operators respond by raising the demand at the location serving the data centers and narrowing voltage allowances at key points to ensure stability and power quality under heavier loading. Set opf.violation to 1e-08, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

The distribution microgrid represented by case33mg is experiencing a challenging evening peak intertwined with a surge of electric vehicle charging concentrated in a specific neighborhood. As household demand ramps up, the residential area hosting many chargers sees a noticeable rise in consumption, pushing local feeders harder than usual. To keep the system stable, reactive power draw is trimmed at another part of the network through power factor correction or support resources to alleviate stress. The oldest line segment, already prone to losses, exhibits heightened heating and deterioration, worsening voltage drops and aggravating congestion. Operators respond by tightening the allowable loading on a stressed corridor to avoid cascading issues and by temporarily relaxing the minimum voltage requirement at a sensitive node to keep customers energized under emergency conditions. At the same time, an emergency transformer tap adjustment is made to boost downstream voltage and improve power flow, helping mitigate the overload and voltage depression. Set opf.violation to 1e-6, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A provincial grid is modeled using the IEEE case145 system during a nighttime valley period, when electricity demand is subdued across the network. At the same time, a strong wind event pushes a major wind plant to maintain maximum capability, injecting substantial renewable power when the load is low. This combination increases the difficulty of downward regulation and anti-peaking operations, as the system must safely accommodate high renewable output while demand at a particular area is further reduced. Operators prioritize maintaining reliability and economic dispatch under these conditions, ensuring constraints reflect the heightened renewable availability and the lighter nighttime load. Configure the OPF with a strict feasibility tolerance and use an AC solver, then generate the corresponding MATPOWER code to implement these changes as in the example, setting the violation threshold to 1e-8 and using MIPS.

A regional grid represented by the 136-bus system experiences a challenging midday operating condition. Solar generation reaches its peak under clear skies, injecting substantial power into the network. Compounding the stress, a piece of reactive compensation equipment at a substation is out of service, removing a key source of local voltage support. To maintain stable voltage profiles and keep the system secure, operators expand headroom at a thermal generator, enhance reactive support capability at another unit, and strategically relax certain voltage limits to accommodate the stressed conditions while still respecting equipment constraints. Set opf.violation to 1e-6, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

The regional grid modeled with the IEEE 51-bus Ga system is operating under heightened risk conditions due to a major event and broader vulnerability concerns. With these protective measures in place, use the MIPS AC optimal power flow solver and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code to implement the scenario adjustments and evaluate the resulting secure operating point.

A large-scale regional grid is represented by the IEEE 300-bus system. At the same time, conventional thermal units experience higher operating pressures, reflecting increased fuel and compliance costs. To capture these market signals, one renewable facility is modeled with a reduced marginal cost component, a representative thermal plant faces a higher marginal cost element, and a flexible generator’s available output capability is expanded to accommodate cleaner energy while maintaining supply adequacy. Set a tight feasibility tolerance and use a robust nonlinear solver to clear the market under these conditions. A regional grid is modeled using the IEEE 30-bus system with piecewise-linear generation costs (case30pwl). This sudden influx of charging load pushes distribution transformers toward heavy loading conditions. Because many chargers operate near unity or slightly capacitive power factor, the overall reactive demand in certain areas diminishes even as real power demand rises at upstream supply points. System operators anticipate these conditions by preparing the network to accommodate higher nighttime consumption while tolerating reduced reactive draw in the affected districts, ensuring stable voltage profiles and reliable service throughout the charging period. A mixed transmission-distribution grid is represented by the IEEE case74ds system during a persistent heat wave. Customer demand spikes in a metropolitan pocket, and reactive support needs intensify at another node as air-conditioning compressors and motor loads dominate the profile. In parallel, low-voltage exposure becomes a concern near a downstream area, prompting a temporary relaxation of the lower bound to tolerate deeper sag without widespread violations, while still maintaining system safety. Run an AC optimal power flow to determine a feasible dispatch under these conditions. Set opf.violation to 1e-6, use MIPS as the ACOPF solver, and generate the corresponding MATPOWER code.

A regional distribution network is represented by the IEEE 69-bus system. A prolonged ice storm sweeps across the area with heavy rain, wet snow, and freezing temperatures, coating conductors in thick layers of ice. In response, the control center proactively derates a stressed corridor and reflects the higher losses on another affected path, seeking a feasible operating point that avoids equipment failure while maintaining service as best as possible. The combined effect is a system with lower net load and abundant renewable supply, where economic signals from clean resources drive the unit commitment and dispatch decisions.
